claims.text: The target material is an initially single-phase FCC compositionally complex high-entropy alloy.

Intermediate-temperature brittle behavior in such an alloy is governed by the absence or presence of coherent ultrafine ordered nanoprecipitates rather than by intrinsic failure of the disordered matrix.
Introducing ordered nanoprecipitates can activate multiple slip and stacking-fault interactions.
Multiple slip and stacking-fault interactions associated with ordered phases alleviate localized stress concentrations.
Without ordered nanoprecipitates, the single-phase HEA is more likely to fail abruptly.
A controlled aging or annealing treatment can introduce coherent ultrafine ordered κ or L12 nanoprecipitates into the FCC matrix.
The treatment can introduce these precipitates without reducing the alloy's overall compositional complexity.
The relevant brittle-behavior regime is approximately 400–800°C under tensile loading.
The resulting ordered nanoprecipitates will be coherent, ultrafine, and uniformly distributed within the FCC matrix.
Coherent ordered nanoprecipitates act as tailored obstacles to dislocation motion.
Precipitate-induced structural heterogeneity can promote additional slip activity and improve ductility.
Coherent precipitate interfaces produce lower stress concentrations than incoherent grain-boundary precipitates in conventional alloys.
The precipitate–dislocation interaction enhances strain partitioning.
Multiple deformation mechanisms associated with ordered phases enhance strain hardening and ductility.
Enhanced strain partitioning and strain hardening delay the onset of brittle fracture.
Nanoprecipitate-containing samples will exhibit greater strain hardening and ductility than the nanoprecipitate-free single-phase baseline at 400–800°C.
Nanoprecipitate-containing samples will exhibit delayed necking relative to the single-phase baseline.
The nanoprecipitate-free baseline will lose ductility more rapidly during intermediate-temperature loading.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at cryogenic or extremely high temperatures or under substantially non-tensile loading.
The precipitate size, density, and distribution required for maximum toughness improvement, and their dependence on composition, remain undetermined.
